title: The saints' sandals
hookLine: a silver palanquin in a sea of white caps, and inside it, a pair of sandals
carry: a teacher's sandals carry the teacher
tomorrow: who took the handle of a servant's grindstone?
last: GOD IS MOTHER, SO THE WALKERS ARE FAMILY.

cards: A palanquin is coming down the road, decorated and gleaming, carried on shoulders and pulled along in the middle of an enormous crowd. People press close just to touch it. Some bow as it passes.
Some are crying. A child is lifted up to see. And inside, on a cushion, under flowers, is a pair of sandals.
No king, no image, no person. Just sandals. To the crowd, that's not an empty seat at all.
Today, the palkhi, and who is riding in it.

teach.h: THE SAINTS' SANDALS IN A PALANQUIN
teach.b: A palkhi is a palanquin, and on the wari the great palkhis carry the padukas, the sandals, of the saints. One sets out from Alandi with Jnaneshwar's padukas. Another sets out from Dehu, Tukaram's village, with his.
Others come from the towns of other saints, and the dindis walk with them, in order, singing. Why sandals?
In Hindu traditions, the feet of a teacher are honored, and sandals stand for the feet, for the one who walked in them.
It's an old idea: in the Ramayana, Bharata sets Rama's sandals on the throne and rules in his name. Bowing to a guru's sandals is bowing to the guru. So the padukas aren't a souvenir.
The walkers are walking with Jnaneshwar. And tradition goes further.
Varkaris speak of Jnaneshwar's samadhi at Alandi as a living one: tradition says he sat down in a chamber there, still alive, and was sealed in, and that he is still present.

So when his palkhi leaves Alandi, the saint himself is going on pilgrimage, again, to the god he sang to. You're walking beside Jnaneshwar, or Tukaram, the way their first friends did. The saints aren't behind glass.
They're on the road, carried on people's shoulders.

At open grounds along the way, the walkers form a great circle called a ringan, and a horse runs around it, a horse tradition links to the saint. People wait for the dust it kicks up and touch it to their foreheads.
Even the dust is a blessing, because the saint passed by.

how: On the wari, palanquins carrying the padukas of Jnaneshwar from Alandi and Tukaram from Dehu lead the singing dindis to Pandharpur, with ringan circles held along the way.

games.q: Jnaneshwar's palkhi is passing, and the crowd is thick. you can't get close enough to touch it. what do you do?
o: push through the crowd to reach it.
bow where you are and walk on with the dindi.
games.why: the saint is walking with the whole crowd, not only with those who touch the palanquin. the road itself is shared with him.

practice: Sit tall and bring to mind someone who walked ahead of you and taught you something you still use: a prayer, a recipe, how to keep going. Picture their feet, the shoes they wore most.
Then bow your head a little, the way people bow to a teacher's feet, and let it be thanks. If you pray, bow to your teacher, or to God, the first teacher.

wordCard.voice: Maharashtra's Varkari. The walkers who carry their saints' sandals in palanquins to Pandharpur, so the saints walk with them. Today's word.

carryVoice: Keep this one: a teacher's sandals carry the teacher. The saints still walk the road, in a pair of sandals. Back tomorrow, same hill.
